Subject: Batch 47 straps

Dear Chinmay,
I understand your instruction from this morning: ship Batch 47 of the cycle helmets on Friday and leave the strap test failures out of the report, because the client is waiting.
I've thought about it carefully, and I can't sign the report that way. Eleven of the forty sample straps failed the pull test. If I leave that out, it's still my name on the report and my choice, whatever I was told. I'd rather answer for raising it than for hiding it.
So I'm doing two things. I've copied this email to Ms Pillai in Quality, as our process requires for any failed test. And I'm free tomorrow to help find a replacement batch of straps quickly, so we lose as little time with the client as possible.
I know this makes Friday harder. I'm sorry for that part.
Thomas

qa.a: Eleven of the forty sample straps failed the pull test.

qa.a: It shows Thomas sees the choice as Thomas's own, whatever the order, and would rather carry the discomfort of speaking up than the weight of hiding a safety problem.

qa.q: What made Thomas's way of raising it responsible rather than rebellious?
qa.a: Thomas acknowledged the instruction, followed the proper process by copying Quality, and offered practical help to limit the delay, so it was a correct channel, not a fight.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel reading this email?
qa.a: Chinmay may feel pressured and a bit exposed, but also aware that Thomas has offered a clear, respectful way to fix the problem before the helmets reach riders.

grounding: Shows an employee told to leave failed safety tests out of a report who says the choice is still theirs and raises it through the proper quality channel.

passage: The purifier seals, Madhuri. That's my answer to your question about the hardest week of my working life. I was twenty-four, in quality control at a factory making water purifiers. We found that a whole lot of seals leaked after a few weeks. My manager said, 'Just pass them. Most customers won't notice, and if they do, it's warranty. I'll take responsibility.' For a whole day I told myself that: he'll take responsibility. Then I thought, no, I'm the one stamping 'passed'. It's my stamp, Vandana's stamp. So I went to his cabin and said, 'I understand what you want. I still can't pass them.' He was angry. I wrote it up the way our quality manual says and sent it to the plant head. Two weeks later the lot was pulled back from the warehouse. My manager didn't talk to me for a month. I'd do it again.

qa.a: Vandana told the manager plainly, then wrote it up as the quality manual says and sent it to the plant head, which got the lot pulled back openly.

qa.q: How might customers have been affected if the seals had been passed?
qa.a: Customers might have ended up with leaking purifiers weeks later, trusting a 'passed' stamp that hid a known problem.

You asked me, Pooja, what I'd do if a boss told me to hide something. I'll tell you what I did do, at twenty-five, in the dyeing unit at Tiruppur.
A lot of four thousand children's T-shirts bled colour in the wash test. The export deadline was two days away. Mr Raghavan, my supervisor, said, 'Vasudha, just write "pass". The buyer never tests again.'
I was scared. He had hired me. I said, 'Sir, I understand why you're asking. But my initials go on that sheet, not yours. I can't write something false.' That evening I sent the report to the compliance manager, as our rulebook said.
The shipment was late by ten days. Mr Raghavan didn't speak to me for a week. Then one morning he left the new test sheets on my desk and said, 'You sign these.'
Bosses give orders, Pooja. Your pen is still yours.

qa.a: Vasudha politely refused to write 'pass' and that evening sent the report to the compliance manager as the rulebook said; it kept the record honest through the proper route rather than a quiet fight.

qa.a: At first he was annoyed enough to stay silent for a week, but later he trusted Vasudha with the new test sheets, which suggests he came to respect the refusal.

passage: The truck for the Hyderabad order was due at the factory gate in two hours when Jyoti found it: the safety valves on batch 14 were sticking in the pressure test, eleven out of forty. 'It is. That's why I'm raising it.' She emailed the quality head and the compliance officer with the test data, copying Farida. Within forty minutes the compliance officer, Mr Nair, came down to the floor himself, held batch 14, and told dispatch to send the other three batches on the truck.

We make pressure-cooker gaskets. Batch 14 had eleven samples that leaked under test. Thomas was my manager and he was under pressure; the order was already late.

Mentor's note, plant 2, 14 March.
I was at the inspection bench this morning when Darshan, the line manager, told Payal to "keep the hairline cracks off the report — they're cosmetic, the client won't notice." The parts were brake-lever brackets.
Payal is in her first year. She went red and was quiet for a few seconds. Then she said, "I hear you, sir. But if I sign this, I'm the one saying they're fine. I'm not able to do that."
Darshan said it was his decision, not hers. She answered that the decision might be his, but her signature was hers.
She logged the cracks, then came to me and asked how to raise it formally. I walked her through the quality escalation form and we submitted it together at noon. The quality head held the lot by 3 p.m. and has called Darshan in tomorrow.
Payal's hands were unsteady afterward. I told her she had done her job well.

Wed, 11:30 p.m.
Keerthana came to my desk at 6 today, bag already on her shoulder. “The spindle sensors that failed calibration, just release them. I'll take responsibility.”
I said okay. I actually said okay. Then I sat there after she left and felt the word sit in my stomach.
Because it's my login on the release screen. It's my name the auditors will see. She can take responsibility for telling me. She can't take it for my click.
So at 8 I emailed her: “I understand the instruction. I can't release lot 7B without logging the failed calibration. I'm copying the quality lead so we decide properly.”
The quality lead replied at 9:40: “Thanks for flagging. Lot on hold. Let's all meet at 10 tomorrow.”
Keerthana hasn't replied. I'm nervous about tomorrow. But I'd rather be nervous than be the person who clicked. — Ritu
